title: Smart Mobs: The Next Social Revolution

facts.claim: Rheingold: 'Smart mobs emerge when communication and computing technologies amplify human talents for cooperation.' Smart mobs consist of people able to act in concert even if they do not know each other.
facts.source: chapter-1 reading blog; Wikipedia quoting book

facts.claim: Rheingold interviewed dozens of young people on Tokyo streets about texting and keitai (mobile phones) and accompanied flocks of teenagers as they converged on public places coordinated by text messages.
facts.source: reading blog; Edge piece by Rheingold

facts.claim: Anthropologist Mizuko Ito, cited in the book, argues phones freed youth from 'the tyranny of the land line shared by inquisitive family members'. Her team noted over 90 percent of Tokyo teenagers have cell phones.
New norm: texting someone counts as being present, and arriving late is acceptable if you stay in contact by text.
NTT DoCoMo designed and marketed i-mode for youth, sold as fashion and technology; one user quoted calls the phone a 'remote control for your life'.
Tokyo and Helsinki teens, nicknamed thumb tribes for texting with their thumbs, are described as early smart mobs.

Philippines, January 2001: a text message, quoted as 'Go 2EDSA, Wear blck', circulated among citizens; crowds gathered at the EDSA Shrine and President Estrada was removed from office. Rheingold cites it as an example of text-coordinated crowds deposing a government.
facts.source: Stanford class page; Rheingold on Edge; Tilly chapter; Wikipedia

facts.claim: Crowd and message counts for the Estrada protest differ between sources (tens of thousands that night, over a million over days). No number is used.
Rheingold uses the word 'mob' deliberately because of its dark resonances; he notes the same networks can serve terrorists and criminal networks ('netwar').

Helsinki: a group of Finns in their twenties, funded by an American entrepreneur, built a 'shared urban living space' combining a physical location, a virtual community, a mobile social network and a cooperative organization; 300 members a year after launch. Stockholm: fare-jumpers use SMS to warn each other about ticket inspectors on a train; party organizers text their address books and guests must show the message at the door.
Seattle anti-WTO protesters used constantly updated websites, mobile phones and swarming tactics; UK drivers organized spontaneous fuel-price protests with mobile communications.
Rheingold (p. 176 as quoted) compares 'computer-wearing social networks of thinking, communicating humans' to the swarm intelligence of ants, bees, fish and birds.
facts.source: Stanford class page quoting the book

facts.claim: NTT DoCoMo hired a former magazine launch employee for i-mode marketing; WTO protesters in Seattle used SMS, mobile phones and the internet to organize.
